questions.text:
A car drives from Auckland towards Hamilton. It covers 120 km in the first 1.5 hours, then stops for 30 minutes for petrol, then drives a further 30 km in 0.5 hours.

What is its AVERAGE speed for the WHOLE journey (including the stop), in km/h?
questions.markingGuide:
The correct answer is 60 km/h.

Here's why:
Total distance = 120 km + 30 km = 150 km.
Total time = 1.5 h + 0.5 h (stop) + 0.5 h = 2.5 h.
Average speed = total distance ÷ total time = 150 ÷ 2.5 = 60 km/h.
A common mistake is to forget to include the stopped time — but average speed for a JOURNEY includes all of it.
Exam tip: Always read carefully for words like 'whole journey' and 'average'.

questions.text:
Two forces act horizontally on a 5 kg shopping trolley: a 30 N forward push and a 12 N backward friction force.

Using F = ma, what is the trolley's acceleration?
questions.markingGuide:
The correct answer is 3.6 m/s² forwards.

Here's why:
Resultant (net) force = 30 N − 12 N = 18 N forwards (the friction force opposes motion).
Newton's second law: F = ma, so a = F ÷ m = 18 ÷ 5 = 3.6 m/s² forwards.
A common mistake is to use the 30 N push as the force, ignoring friction.
Exam tip: ALWAYS find the NET (resultant) force first before using F = ma.

questions.text: A 2 kg ball is held 5 m above the ground (g = 10 N/kg) and then released. Just before it hits the ground, what is its kinetic energy? (Ignore air resistance.)
questions.markingGuide:
The correct answer is 100 J.

Here's why:
Gravitational PE at the start = mgh = 2 × 10 × 5 = 100 J.
By the law of conservation of energy, with no air resistance, ALL of the GPE is converted to KE just before impact.
So the kinetic energy just before hitting the ground = 100 J.
Exam tip: 'energy is conserved' lets you skip messy speed calculations and just track total energy.

questions.text: Manapōuri is one of NZ's largest hydroelectric power stations. Which row CORRECTLY traces the energy transformations from the reservoir to the national grid, AND identifies where most of the 'lost' energy goes?
options: GPE → KE → electrical; lost energy mainly as heat and sound (friction in turbines and generators)
Chemical → heat → electrical; lost energy as light
Nuclear → heat → electrical; lost energy as gravity
Sound → kinetic → electrical; lost energy as chemical energy
questions.expectedAnswer: GPE → KE → electrical; lost energy mainly as heat and sound (friction in turbines and generators)
questions.markingGuide:
The correct answer is the GPE → KE → electrical option with heat/sound losses.

Here's why:
Water stored at height in the reservoir has gravitational potential energy. Falling through penstocks converts GPE → kinetic energy (the moving water). The kinetic energy spins turbines connected to generators, which convert KE → electrical energy.
No conversion is 100% efficient — friction in the bearings and generators produces heat, and the spinning machinery produces sound. These are the main 'wasted' forms of energy.
Exam tip: NZ generates about 80% of its electricity from renewable sources, with hydroelectric being the largest contributor.

questions.text: In a circuit, two resistors are connected in series with a 12 V battery. R1 = 3 Ω and R2 = 5 Ω. Calculate the CURRENT flowing through the circuit. Give your answer in amps to 2 decimal places.
questions.markingGuide:
Step 1: In a series circuit, total resistance is the SUM of the resistors: R_total = 3 + 5 = 8 Ω.

Step 2: Use Ohm's Law: V = I × R, rearranged to I = V / R.

Step 3: I = 12 ÷ 8 = 1.5 A.

Step 4: Accept 1.5 (or 1.50).

Exam tip: Series → resistances add. Parallel → resistance gets smaller. Always work out total resistance first before applying Ohm's Law.

questions.text:
Two students are arguing about Christmas tree lights:
• Student A says 'You should wire them in series so they share the voltage and don't burn out.'
• Student B says 'You should wire them in parallel so if one bulb fails, the rest still work.'

Explain which student is correct AND describe what happens to the CURRENT and VOLTAGE in each type of circuit. Give ONE other real-world example of where each type of circuit is used.
questions.markingGuide:
1 mark — Series circuit description: components are connected one after another in a single loop. The CURRENT is the same at every point in the circuit, but the VOLTAGE is shared (split) between the components. If one component breaks, the whole circuit is broken and everything stops working.

1 mark — Parallel circuit description: components are connected on separate branches. The VOLTAGE across each branch is the same (= the supply voltage). The CURRENT is split between the branches and adds back together. If one branch breaks, the others keep working.

1 mark — Which student is correct + examples: Student B is correct in modern lighting — parallel wiring is better because one failed bulb does not stop the whole string. Real-world examples: Series — old-style cheap fairy lights, the cells inside a torch, a security alarm loop. Parallel — household wiring (each appliance gets full mains voltage and can be switched independently), modern LED string lights, car headlights.

Exam tip: Most real-world wiring is parallel — your house is parallel so that turning off the kitchen light doesn't turn off the TV.

questions.text:
A student is at one end of a 200 m school field. They watch the PE teacher 200 m away start a stopwatch and fire a starter pistol. Light from the smoke and the BANG travel through the air.

(a) State the speed of light and the speed of sound in air (approximate values).
(b) Explain why the student SEES the smoke before they HEAR the bang.
(c) Calculate roughly how long the bang takes to reach the student. (Show working.)
questions.markingGuide:
1 mark for (a) and (b) combined — must give approximate values: speed of light ≈ 300,000,000 m/s (3×10⁸ m/s); speed of sound in air ≈ 340 m/s. Light reaches the observer almost instantly because it travels nearly a million times faster than sound, so the eye sees the smoke/flash before the ear receives the sound waves.

1 mark for (c) — sound travel time = distance ÷ speed = 200 ÷ 340 ≈ 0.59 s. Accept 0.58–0.6 s with working shown.

Exam tip: 'count the seconds between lightning and thunder, divide by 3 to get distance in km' uses exactly the same idea — sound travels about 340 m every second, so 3 seconds ≈ 1 km.

questions.text:
The velocity-time graph above shows the journey of a cyclist.

Using the graph:
(a) Describe the cyclist's motion in EACH of the three phases of the journey.
(b) Calculate the ACCELERATION during phase 1 (speeding up). Include units.
(c) Calculate the TOTAL DISTANCE covered during the whole journey (use the area under the line).
(d) Calculate the cyclist's AVERAGE speed for the whole journey.
questions.markingGuide:
1 mark (a): Phase 1 (0–5 s) — accelerates uniformly from 0 to 10 m/s. Phase 2 (5–10 s) — travels at constant velocity of 10 m/s. Phase 3 (10–15 s) — decelerates uniformly from 10 m/s to 0.

1 mark (b): Acceleration = change in velocity ÷ time = (10 − 0) ÷ 5 = 2 m/s². Must include the unit m/s².

1 mark (c) and (d): Distance = area under graph (trapezium) = ½ × (5 + 15) × 10 = 100 m. (Or split into triangle + rectangle + triangle: 25 + 50 + 25 = 100 m.)
Average speed = total distance ÷ total time = 100 m ÷ 15 s ≈ 6.67 m/s.

Must show working in (b), (c) and (d).

Exam tip: On a velocity-time graph, the GRADIENT gives acceleration and the AREA under the line gives distance travelled.

questions.text:
New Zealand experiences frequent earthquakes. Earthquakes produce seismic waves — P-waves (primary) and S-waves (secondary).

Explain TWO important DIFFERENCES between P-waves and S-waves. Then describe how the BEHAVIOUR of these waves provides scientific evidence for the structure of the Earth's interior (specifically, what the difference tells us about the OUTER CORE).
questions.markingGuide:
1 mark — First difference (wave type): P-waves are LONGITUDINAL (particles vibrate parallel to the direction the wave is travelling — compressions and rarefactions). S-waves are TRANSVERSE (particles vibrate at right angles to the direction of travel).

1 mark — Second difference (speed and medium): P-waves travel FASTER than S-waves and arrive at seismograph stations FIRST (hence 'primary'). P-waves can travel through both SOLIDS and LIQUIDS, but S-waves can ONLY travel through SOLIDS.

1 mark — Evidence for Earth's structure: Seismographs on the side of the Earth opposite to an earthquake DETECT P-waves but NOT S-waves. The only explanation is that S-waves are blocked by something on the way through. Because S-waves cannot travel through liquids, this is evidence that the OUTER CORE of the Earth is LIQUID. P-waves also bend (refract) as they pass between layers of different density, which is how we know the Earth has distinct layers (crust, mantle, outer core, inner core).

Exam tip: This is one of the best examples in Year 10 of how indirect evidence (waves we can detect at the surface) lets scientists 'see' inside something we can't dig down to.

questions.text:
A wind turbine generates 2,000,000 J (2 MJ) of electrical energy in 100 seconds. The turbine is rated at 30% efficiency — meaning only 30% of the kinetic energy of the wind hitting the blades is converted to electrical energy.

(a) Calculate the POWER OUTPUT of the wind turbine, in watts.
(b) Calculate the TOTAL kinetic energy of the wind that struck the turbine in those 100 seconds.
(c) Explain, using the law of conservation of energy, where the 'lost' energy goes.
(d) Compare wind power with fossil fuel power stations: give ONE clear ADVANTAGE and ONE clear DISADVANTAGE of wind power for NZ's electricity supply.
questions.markingGuide:
1 mark (a): Power = energy ÷ time = 2,000,000 ÷ 100 = 20,000 W (or 20 kW). Must show working.

1 mark (b): Efficiency = useful output ÷ total input × 100. Rearranged: Total input = useful output ÷ efficiency = 2,000,000 ÷ 0.30 ≈ 6,666,667 J (about 6.67 MJ). Accept 6.6–6.7 MJ with working shown.

1 mark (c): The law of conservation of energy says energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transformed. The 'missing' 70% (≈ 4.67 MJ) is converted to other forms — heat in the gears and bearings (friction), sound (turbines are noisy), and importantly some kinetic energy stays in the air leaving the turbine (you can't extract 100% of the wind's energy or the air would have to stop completely behind the blades). The TOTAL energy is conserved — it is just spread across multiple forms.

1 mark (d): ONE clear advantage AND ONE clear disadvantage with reasoning.

Advantages (any one): renewable resource that won't run out; produces no CO₂ during operation, helping NZ reach 100% renewable electricity; reduces need for imported fossil fuels; wind is free; well-suited to NZ's high-wind sites (Cook Strait, Manawatū Gorge).

Disadvantages (any one): wind is intermittent (variable and unreliable, so backup power is needed on calm days); turbines can be visually intrusive; can affect bird and bat populations; high upfront cost; remote sites need long transmission lines.

Exam tip: No energy conversion is 100% efficient — heat and sound are the most common 'waste' forms. Excellence-level answers always link this back to conservation of energy.
